Executive summaryHPE's AI-cycle re-rating has run ahead of what its cash flows support

HPE has changed more in eighteen months than in its first decade as a listed company. The $13.6bn Juniper acquisition made networking 26% of revenue and 40% of segment profit, and an AI-driven server cycle lifted trailing revenue +31% with record margins. The share price tripled from its February low to $62.09 on 2026-09-11. Our work finds a better business than the one the market valued at 7–10x earnings, but not yet one whose cash flows justify $62.09 unless today's peak-cycle margins become permanent.

What the market is pricing in

$62.09

Calculated 13.5x FY27 consensus non-GAAP EPS of $4.60, against HPE's own 4–10x history S033.

Calculated Reverse DCF: a long-term non-GAAP operating margin of 18.4% at base-case growth, or a 10.8% revenue CAGR to FY36 at base margins, or a 7.0% cost of capital.

Interpretation The market is capitalising HPE partly at AI-hardware peer multiples (Dell 23.0x next-year P/E).

What the fundamental evidence suggests

$35–$43

Calculated Base-case DCF $38.80 per fully diluted share (WACC 9.30% ±0.5pp, terminal growth ±0.25pp); scenario range $22 bear to $54 bull; probability-weighted $38.43.

Calculated Cross-checks: Damodaran FCFF Ginzu $31.57; HPE's own forward P/E history $20–$46.

Interpretation Relative value at today's peer multiples ($67–$106) is the case for the price — it assumes the sector's multiples hold.

Key conclusions

  • The business mix has measurably improved. Calculated Networking earned a 22.7% TTM segment margin versus 12.6% in Cloud & AI; TTM after-tax adjusted ROIC of 11.2% is above our 9.3% WACC for the first time in the six years we reviewed.
  • Part of the margin surge is cyclical. Reported Q3 FY26 non-GAAP gross margin hit 40.4% on disciplined pricing amid memory shortages; management itself expects gross margin to "moderate toward more historical levels" S066. Interpretation Pass-through pricing that lifted revenue can reverse when DRAM contract prices (+13–18% QoQ in 3Q26) normalise S147.
  • Demand visibility is strong but concentrated in AI. Reported Record AI backlog of $7.6bn, a post-quarter $3.5bn hyperscaler inference deal and an Oracle networking agreement support the raised FY27 framework (revenue +13–17%, free cash flow ≥$5bn) S065.
  • Financial health is adequate, not pristine. Calculated Net debt $14.0bn is 1.75x TTM adjusted EBITDA (company: 1.8x); inventory has almost doubled to $11.8bn and is financed by payables; the mandatory convertible adds 8.8% to the share count with employee awards and the Oracle warrant.
  • Valuation is the decisive question. Calculated At $62.09 the stock sits above every intrinsic method and below every peer-multiple method we ran — the outcome hinges on whether HPE earns a structurally higher multiple, not on the next quarter.

Reading the chart. The methods separate into two groups. Cash-flow methods form narrow bars to the left of the price line: base DCF $35–43 on WACC ±0.5pp and terminal growth ±0.25pp, scenarios $22–54. Peer-multiple methods form much wider bars ($35–106 on next-year P/E, $19–84 on EV/EBITDA) that straddle or exceed the price. The width difference is mechanical: peer multiples themselves range from 7.5x (Supermicro) to 38.7x (Arista), so a relative method inherits the dispersion of the comparator set, while the DCF range reflects only the flexed discount rate and terminal growth.

Variables that will prove or disprove the thesis

  • Cloud & AI margin after memory normalises — management frames FY27 at ~13%; holding ≥13% through a falling DRAM price cycle would support the bull case.
  • Networking growth and margin — FY27 +14–17% at a "mid-to-high 20%" margin; the Networking Investor Day on 30-Sep-2026 is the next test.
  • Conversion of the $7.6bn AI backlog into FY27 free cash flow of ≥$5bn without further inventory build.
  • Sector multiples — HPE's price leans on Dell, Cisco and NetApp trading at 18–23x next-year earnings.

Interpretation We would move our fundamental range materially higher if HPE demonstrated a long-term non-GAAP operating margin of 15% or more (for example networking above 35% of revenue with Cloud & AI holding 13%), and lower if non-GAAP gross margin fell back below 33% or AI backlog declined sequentially.

1 · Business overviewFrom server vendor to a networking-led infrastructure company

Reported Hewlett Packard Enterprise sells the hardware, software and services that enterprises, governments and cloud providers use to run data centres and campus networks. Since the first quarter of FY26 it reports two operating segments plus a residual: Cloud & AI (servers including AI systems, storage, and HPE Financial Services) and Networking (HPE Aruba and Juniper: campus & branch, data-centre switching, security and routing) S063. Revenue is recognised mostly on shipment of products, with services and financing recognised over time.

Cloud & AI is flat to falling until Q1 FY26 and then rises from $6.3bn to $9.0bn in two quarters, which is where the AI-systems and pricing effect appears. Reading the chart. Revenue is concentrated: Server alone is $21.0bn, 50% of the group, and the four Cloud & AI lines total about 71%. Growth is concentrated in the smaller networking lines: Routing +270% year on year at $3.2bn, data-centre networking +112% at $1.5bn and Security +76% at $1.1bn, all of which reflect the first full year of Juniper rather than organic expansion. Financial Services is the only line that is flat (−0.3%), consistent with a lease book that turns over slowly.

Recurring versus transactional revenue

Reported About two-thirds of revenue is transactional hardware. Services (34% of FY25 revenue), financing income and subscription-like GreenLake contracts are recurring. HPE's annualised revenue run-rate (ARR) — GreenLake cloud services, financing and software/SaaS — was $3,151m at FY25 year-end, up 63% largely because Juniper's software support revenue was added S029. Management targeted ARR of about $3.5bn by the end of FY26 and reported 52,000 GreenLake customers in Q3 FY26, up 18% S074S066.

Customer stickiness and switching costs

Interpretation Stickiness differs sharply by business. Networking is the stickiest: campus networks are managed through Aruba Central or Juniper Mist cloud platforms, embedded in security policy and operations, and refreshed on multi-year cycles, and routing platforms use HPE's own Express 5 silicon. Storage and GreenLake carry moderate switching costs from data gravity and multi-year consumption contracts, reflected in $5,561m of deferred revenue. Servers — half of revenue — are largely interchangeable x86 and GPU systems bought competitively, which is why IDC shows HPE growing slower than Dell, Supermicro and Lenovo S140. Churn risk is therefore highest in the largest revenue line and lowest in the most profitable one.

IDC's AI-infrastructure figure counts servers and storage bought for AI workloads; Gartner's data-centre systems category adds networking and non-AI servers; switching trackers measure one product family. Reading the chart. The distribution is dominated by ODM-direct shipments at $89.7bn, 53.9% of the market, which go straight from contract manufacturers to hyperscalers and are effectively outside HPE's addressable market. Among OEMs, Dell is $22.2bn and grew 165%, Supermicro $10.2bn (+97%) and Lenovo $8.4bn (+100%), against HPE at $5.9bn (+46%). Since the total market grew 52%, HPE's growth below that rate is a decline in share, from about 3.9% to 3.5%. IEIT is the only vendor with negative growth (−8%).

Porter's five forces

ForceIntensityHPE-specific evidence
Rivalry among competitorsHighDell (13.4% server share), Supermicro and Lenovo grow faster in AI servers; Cisco, Arista and NVIDIA contest data-centre networking; ODMs supply hyperscalers directly.
Supplier powerHighNVIDIA/AMD accelerators, a three-firm memory industry (Micron gross margin 85%) and Broadcom switch silicon set cost and allocation. HPE's own routing silicon is a partial offset.
Buyer powerMedium–highHyperscalers, neoclouds and sovereign programmes buy in very large, competitively bid lots; enterprise buyers are fragmented but price-aware.
Threat of substitutesMediumPublic-cloud IaaS substitutes for on-premises infrastructure; HPE's counter is on-premises inference economics (claimed up to 60% lower token cost).
Threat of new entrantsLow–mediumScale, supply allocations and channel reach deter entry, but white-box/ODM systems and vertically integrated GPU vendors lower the barrier in AI clusters.

Interpretation The structure explains HPE's history: strong suppliers and powerful buyers squeeze server economics, and the industry's profit pool sits with silicon vendors and differentiated networking. The Juniper acquisition is best read as a deliberate move toward the part of the stack with pricing power.

Reading the chart. Combined quarterly capital expenditure of Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle rises from $36.6bn in 2023Q1 to $181.5bn in 2026Q2, about five times. The series is convex: growth is roughly flat through 2023, turns positive in 2024 and steepens from 2024Q4, with trailing-twelve-month growth reaching +81%. All five contribute, with Amazon largest at $54.2bn in the final quarter and Oracle the fastest-growing from a small base. There is no flattening in the data, which is why the report treats a capex pause as a scenario rather than an observed trend.

Reading the chart. Micron's gross margin traces a full memory cycle: about 47% in 2021, a collapse to −33% by February 2023 as contract prices fell below cash cost, a recovery through 2024 to the high 30s, and then an acceleration to 84.6% by May 2026. The final four quarters are the steepest part of the series, which places memory pricing at a cyclical extreme rather than at a new plateau. This matters for HPE because memory is one of the largest input costs in a server, so the same conditions that raise Micron's margin raise HPE's component costs and its selling prices.

Interpretation The memory channel deserves the most attention. Micron's gross margin rising from 38% to 85% in a year signals a price spike that HPE has so far passed on — Q3 server revenue grew 35% on ASPs while units were supply-constrained S066. The same mechanism works in reverse: when contract prices fall, server revenue can shrink even with flat unit demand, and inventory bought at peak prices must be sold into a falling market. S&P's stable BBB outlook, affirmed after the Juniper close, gives the balance sheet room to absorb that swing S149.

Reading the chart. The 10-year yield rises from 0.93% in January 2021 to a 4.98% peak in October 2023, then oscillates between roughly 3.6% and 5.0% without returning toward pre-2022 levels, ending at 4.95%. The dollar index peaks at 114 in September 2022 and declines to 99.1. The two series matter to the valuation through different channels: the yield is the risk-free rate in the 9.3% WACC, so the plateau keeps the discount rate high, while the weaker dollar raises the translated value of the 61% of revenue earned outside the United States.

Quantifying the transmission: two driver regressions

Experiment 1 Revenue–capex regression. Hypothesis. If HPE's growth tracks hyperscaler spending, its revenue growth should rise and fall with cloud-capex growth once the Juniper acquisition is accounted for. Method. Quarterly OLS of HPE's year-over-year log revenue growth on the capex growth of Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle (same quarter and two lags) plus a dummy for quarters that include Juniper. We test whether the three capex coefficients jointly sum to zero, then repeat with lags 0–4 and on pre-Juniper quarters only. Data. SEC XBRL, 34 quarters (2018Q1–2026Q2); HPE fiscal quarters aligned to the calendar quarter they mostly cover.

Assumption Both regressions in this section use Newey-West (HAC, 4 lags) standard errors, because year-over-year observations overlap, and t-distribution p-values, because the samples are short (34 and 31 quarters). The Durbin-Watson statistics still show residual autocorrelation, so coefficients are indicative, not precise.

R1 — HPE revenue growth (YoY, log) on cloud-capex growth (MSFT, GOOGL, AMZN, META, ORCL; YoY, log). Sample 2018Q1 to 2026Q2. t-distribution p-values; italic rows test the sum of the capex coefficients.

Calculated No single capex lag is significant on its own (the strongest is lag 1, p = 0.09), but jointly the three lags sum to 0.19 (p = 0.03): a 10-point acceleration in cloud-capex growth has gone with about 1.9 points faster HPE revenue growth over three quarters. A similar sum appears before Juniper (0.18, p = 0.03), although that fit is weak (R² 0.27). The link is fragile: allowing lags 0–4 cuts the sum to 0.09 (p = 0.45). Quarters that include Juniper grew 15 points faster than capex explains (p = 0.002); most of the full model's R² of 0.60 comes from that dummy. FY2016 quarters are excluded because their XBRL values straddle the 2017 spin-off restatements. Interpretation Cloud capex is a real but small and unstable demand signal for HPE rather than a driver it captures directly — hyperscalers buy mostly from ODMs — so HPE's 2026 acceleration rests more on enterprise and sovereign AI, pricing and the acquisition than on hyperscaler budgets.

Reading the chart. Across the pre-Juniper sample the relationship is positive but shallow: capex growth ranges from −10% to +65% while HPE's revenue growth stays within roughly ±15%, and the three lags sum to 0.19 (joint p = 0.03). The five quarters that include Juniper sit about 15 percentage points above the fitted line, which is what the dummy measures (p = 0.002). The vertical scatter at high capex growth is wide, and extending the model to lags 0–4 halves the sum and removes significance, so the relationship is small and not robust — consistent with hyperscalers buying mostly ODM-direct rather than from HPE.

Experiment 2 Gross margin–memory regression. Hypothesis. Memory is a large server input cost, so memory-price spikes should squeeze HPE's gross margin unless HPE passes them on in price. Method. Quarterly OLS of the year-over-year change in HPE's GAAP gross margin on the change in Micron's gross margin (our proxy for memory contract prices; same quarter and two lags) plus the Juniper dummy. We repeat it without the dummy and compare the latest quarters with what the model predicts. Data. HPE 10-Q and 10-K statements and Micron XBRL, 31 quarters (2018Q4–2026Q2).

Calculated Each 10-point rise in Micron's gross margin (a proxy for memory contract prices) coincided with a 0.46-point lower change in HPE's gross margin in the same quarter (p = 0.005); Juniper quarters add 6.8 points (p = 0.002). The memory link is not robust: without the Juniper dummy it disappears (−0.007, p = 0.88), because before 2025 the largest memory spikes coincided with the low-margin AI-server ramp of 2024. The latest quarters break the pattern: for Q3 FY26 the model predicts +4.4 points (memory −2.2, Juniper +6.8, constant −0.2) against an actual +10.9 points, leaving +6.5 points unexplained, up from −3.2 points in Q4 FY25 as memory prices climbed. Interpretation The history gives no support to clean pass-through of memory costs: past spikes came with slightly lower margins, if anything. FY26's margin gain lies outside that history and is consistent with the disciplined pricing amid memory shortages that management described S066 — pricing ahead of costs on inventory bought earlier. That is the part of the margin most exposed when the memory cycle turns, which is the asymmetry the bear case relies on.

Reading the chart. The fitted slope is mildly negative: a 10-point rise in Micron's margin coincides with a 0.46-point lower change in HPE's gross margin (p = 0.005 with the Juniper control, p = 0.88 without it). The 2024 points in the lower-right quadrant carry that result, a period when memory prices rose while HPE's margin fell on low-margin AI-server mix. The FY26 points sit well above the line: in Q3 FY26 the actual change was +10.9pp against +4.4pp predicted. The historical relationship therefore does not describe FY26, when HPE priced ahead of its component costs.

Technology: what could change the stack

  • Reported On-premises inference and agentic AI. HPE Private Cloud AI (co-engineered with NVIDIA) is pitched at "up to 60% lower token cost" than public cloud; traditional server orders rose 75% in Q3 as enterprises bought AI-ready configurations S065. Interpretation If inference migrates on-premises, enterprise server refresh cycles lengthen into a multi-year upgrade — HPE's core strength — rather than a hyperscaler-only boom.
  • Reported Scale-out and scale-across networking. Juniper PTX routers with in-house Express 5 silicon and liquid-cooled Tomahawk 6 switches target AI data-centre interconnect; networks-for-AI orders reached $2.2bn cumulatively S066. Interpretation This is the one area where HPE owns silicon, which is where competitive structure changes in its favour.
  • Reported Rack-scale systems. AMD Helios racks with HPE Juniper scale-up switches start ramping around the end of calendar 2026 and are excluded from FY27 guidance. Interpretation Rack-scale designs shift value toward GPU vendors and integrators with liquid-cooling skills (HPE's Cray heritage), but compress server-vendor margins.
  • Interpretation Cost structure. Supply is now the binding constraint for all vendors (Dell'Oro: data-centre switching "supply-constrained rather than demand-constrained") S145; multi-year supply agreements favour large OEMs with balance sheets.

Interpretation Overall, HPE has a narrow moat concentrated in networking and none in its largest revenue line. The best quantitative evidence is return on capital: after-tax adjusted ROIC averaged 8.1% over FY2020–FY2025, below any reasonable cost of capital, before improving to 11.2% in the AI-cycle TTM.

Growth drivers

  • Reported AI systems: $6.8bn backlog plus the $3.5bn post-quarter inference award; 59% of cumulative AI orders from sovereign and enterprise customers.
  • Reported Networks for AI and Oracle: FY26 order target raised to $2.5–3.0bn; Oracle to deploy HPE Juniper routing and switching across its AI data centres S151.
  • Reported Juniper cost synergies: target raised to a $600m annual run-rate by the end of FY28 (originally $450m) S065S186.
  • Reported Pricing: campus switch ASPs +19% YoY industry-wide in 2Q26 S143; server ASPs rising with memory costs.
  • Interpretation Enterprise AI refresh and liquid-cooling demand; Helios scale-up switching as upside not in guidance.

3 · Financial performance & healthFour flat years, then a step change in scale, margins and cash

Calculated Revenue compounded at just 2.8% a year from FY2020 to FY2024, then grew 13.8% in FY2025 (partial-year Juniper) and 30.8% in the four quarters to July 2026. The five-year CAGR to FY2025 is 4.9%. All statement figures below are parsed from the 10-K and 10-Q filings and reconcile to SEC XBRL data to the dollar; FY2020 serves as the growth base S029S001S123.

Pre-Juniper baseline: what an ARIMA model says FY26 "should" have been

Experiment 3 Pre-Juniper revenue baseline. Hypothesis. If FY26 were only a continuation of HPE's pre-Juniper business, actual revenue would stay inside the prediction band of a model fitted before the acquisition. Method. A seasonal ARIMA on log quarterly revenue, order chosen by AICc from a small grid capped at four parameters; a one-step rolling backtest against a random walk and a seasonal-naive forecast, with Diebold-Mariano tests; the forecast from Q3 FY25 compared with actuals; the FY26 excess split into Juniper (estimated from company-normalised growth) and the rest, and recomputed on eight alternative baselines. Data. HPE XBRL revenue, FY2018 Q1–FY2025 Q2: 30 quarters after the 2017 spin-offs and before Juniper.

Assumption The selected model is SARIMA(0,0,1)(0,0,0)₄: essentially HPE's stable pre-deal revenue level with short-lived shocks, so it is a no-growth baseline rather than a trend. Its residuals show no remaining autocorrelation (Ljung-Box p = 0.52). The model is a counterfactual — HPE without the acquisition and the AI cycle — not our forecast.

Reading the chart. For seven years quarterly revenue oscillates between $6.0bn and $8.5bn with no trend, which is why the selected SARIMA(0,0,1) baseline is a flat level of about $7.26bn with a 95% band of $6.4–8.2bn. After the Juniper close the actual series leaves the band immediately and the gap widens monotonically: +22%, +33%, +28%, +47% and +68%. A widening gap rather than a one-off step is what distinguishes a continuing cycle plus consolidation from a single acquisition effect, and it is why the decomposition attributes only 32–38% of the excess to Juniper.

Calculated In backtest the model's mean absolute error (4.8%) is lower than a random walk's (5.8%) and a seasonal-naive forecast's (8.6%), but over eight quarters neither difference is statistically significant (Diebold-Mariano p = 0.44 and 0.08), so we rely on it as a baseline, not as a forecaster. All 5 quarters since the Juniper close sit above its 95% band, and TTM revenue is +44% above the counterfactual. Across eight alternative baselines FY26 no-change revenue ranges from $29.0bn to $31.6bn and Juniper's estimated share of the excess from 32% to 38%; every ARIMA variant also puts all five quarters above its 95% band.

About a third of the break is Juniper; the rest — roughly $11.8bn — is the AI and pricing cycle, which is precisely the part whose persistence the market is paying for and our base case fades.

Reading the chart. Free cash flow does not trend: it moves between $0.6bn and $3.7bn over six years and reaches $4.5bn over the trailing twelve months, with the margin oscillating between 2.1% and 13.4%. The swings are larger than the swings in operating profit, which identifies working capital rather than profitability as the main driver. The FY2025 trough (2.9%) and the current peak (10.7%) both coincide with large inventory and payables movements, so the level is best read with the working-capital chart rather than on its own.

Reading the chart. Days inventory outstanding rises from 52.7 in FY2020 to 162.9, tripling, while days payable outstanding rises from 106 to 189. Days sales outstanding is stable between 44 and 56 throughout. The cash conversion cycle, negative in most earlier years, is +27.6 days. The mechanism is visible in the two series moving together: suppliers are financing the inventory build, so free cash flow holds up while inventory grows. The exposure is the reversal — if payable days normalise faster than inventory days, the cash conversion cycle lengthens and free cash flow falls even with stable profit.

Calculated TTM free cash flow of $4,501m (10.7% of revenue) is the best in HPE's history, but its quality needs care: inventory rose $5,471m since October while payables rose $6,003m. Interpretation Suppliers are financing the AI backlog; if order conversion slows, that financing unwinds and FCF could swing by several billion dollars in either direction.

Capital structure, financing and dilution

Reported HPE has financed itself with investment-grade debt (BBB, stable) and one equity-linked issue: 30.0m shares of 7.625% Series C mandatory convertible preferred ($1.46bn net, September 2024) that convert on or about 1-Sep-2027 into 2.5352–3.1056 common shares each S029S097. No convertible notes or employee option programmes of significance were identified. In March 2026 it issued $2.0bn of senior notes (2028–2033), retired the Juniper term loan with H3C proceeds, and plans to repay $1.25bn of notes in September 2026 S001S066. Authorised common stock is 9.6bn shares; 1,328m were outstanding at 31-Jul-2026.

Maturities are front-loaded: $3.8bn in FY2026, $3.1bn in FY2027 and $4.6bn in FY2028 including the March-2026 issuance, against $2.4bn and $3.0bn combined in FY2029 and only $0.4bn in FY2030. A further $8.9bn sits beyond FY2030. The near-term concentration means refinancing cost, not liquidity, is the exposure: $11.5bn of liquidity covers the next two years, but the FY2026–28 tranches reprice at current yields, which is why the 10-year yield appears in the risk table.

Calculated Dilution is modest: the preferred adds 76.1m shares at the minimum conversion rate, and SBC runs at about 2% of revenue. Reported Management intends to offset SBC dilution with roughly $650m of annual buybacks and to return at least 75% of free cash flow from Q4 FY26, with $3.2bn of authorisation remaining S074S063. Interpretation HPE generates cash, so cash runway is not a relevant constraint. The only foreseeable funding needs are refinancing roughly $3–4bn of maturities a year through FY2028, comfortably covered by FCF guidance and $11.5bn of cash plus undrawn revolver.

Calculated Reverse DCF. Holding everything else at base case, $62.09 requires a long-term non-GAAP operating margin of 18.4% (FY27 guide: 14–15%; FY2020–FY2025 range 8.5%–10.8%), or revenue growth 5.8 percentage points faster every year (a 10.8% ten-year CAGR versus 5.0%), or a 7.0% WACC. Calculated Damodaran cross-check. Aswath Damodaran's FCFF "simple Ginzu" spreadsheet was completed on every relevant sheet — inputs, cost of capital, trailing-12-month worksheet and story — with an added "HPE notes" sheet that sources each input (excel/HPE_Damodaran_fcffsimpleginzu.xlsx). Using Damodaran's own conventions — industry betas weighted by estimated business value (1.21 unlevered), a regional equity risk premium weighted by HPE's revenue (5.27%), and a Baa2/BBB cost of debt — it produces a 11.06% cost of capital and $31.57 per share, against our 9.30% and $38.80. Interpretation The difference comes mainly from the equity risk premium: Damodaran's January-2026 regional table (4.23% mature-market premium plus country risk for HPE's EMEA, Asia and Latin American revenue) versus the 3.97% US implied premium in our build. The Ginzu also converges tax to the 21% marginal rate. Both models sit well below the $62.09 price.

NetApp is a high-quality, slower-growth cash generator. Weakest: Supermicro, with an 11% gross margin and negative trailing free cash flow, has growth without economics. HPE sits between Dell and Cisco: its networking mix gives it nearly twice Dell's gross margin and a stronger FCF margin, but amortisation, SBC and restructuring hold GAAP operating margin at 6.2%, and it is losing server share to Dell, Supermicro and Lenovo. We did not rank by share-price performance.

Reading the chart. For ten years the weekly close oscillates within $5.4–24.6 with no lasting trend, including a 57% drawdown in 2018–2020. From April 2026 the series breaks above that decade-long range and reaches $62.09, roughly 2.5 times the previous high, and the 40-week moving average turns up steeply behind it. On a logarithmic scale a constant growth rate is a straight line, so the visible curvature is an acceleration rather than a continuation. The event markers show that the re-rating follows the Juniper close and the Q2 FY26 results rather than any single announcement.

Reading the chart. The upper panel shows two regimes: a $12.5–26 range until April 2026, then a rise to $62.09 that leaves the price 83% above its 200-day average ($34.01) and the 50-day average ($51.11) far above the 200-day. The middle panel shows volume above twice its 50-day average clustering on earnings dates, with the largest bar on 2-Jun-2026. The lower panel shows RSI(14) repeatedly above 70 from April 2026, peaking near 87 the day before the 2-Jun move. Extended momentum readings describe the distance from trend; they are not used in this report as a timing signal.

Reading the chart. The window covers the re-rating and the consolidation after it. The price roughly triples from about $21 to a peak above $64, with the single largest step on 2-Jun-2026 (+19.5% on 7.4x average volume). Since then it has traded between $40.7 and $64.3 with the 12-day EMA above the 26-day, and Bollinger bandwidth has contracted from 85% to 18%, which measures a narrowing dispersion of daily closes rather than a directional signal. The 11-Sep close of $62.09 is a record close but still below the intraday highs of early June.

Reading the chart. The series returns to zero only at new highs, so the depth and duration of each trough describe the risk of holding the stock. Seven episodes exceed 22%: the deepest is −56.9% from March 2018, which took 748 days to reach its trough and a further 655 to recover; −48.4% in 2025 recovered in 155 days; the most recent, −26.4% from 2-Jun-2026, took 30 days to the trough and 41 to recover. Recovery has become faster as the shareholder base has changed, but the frequency of >20% drawdowns has not fallen, which is the empirical basis for sizing positions to tail risk.

Calculated Five drawdowns exceeded 20% in the last four years, including −48% from January to April 2025 (guidance cut, tariffs) and −26% from June to July 2026. Across 11 earnings releases since March 2024, the average absolute day-0 move was 6.7%, against 2.0% on the other trading days of the same period (tested under Stock reaction around events).

Statistical properties of returns

Experiment 4 Return diagnostics. Hypothesis. If past price moves carried information, daily returns would be autocorrelated; if risk were well behaved, volatility would not cluster and extreme days would be as rare as a normal distribution implies. Method. ADF unit-root tests on prices and returns, Ljung-Box tests on returns and squared returns, Engle's ARCH-LM test, the Jarque-Bera normality test and a count of days beyond three standard deviations. Data. 2,729 daily log returns from HPE's regular-way listing in November 2015 to 11-Sep-2026, adjusted for dividends and spin-offs.

Daily log returns, 2,729 trading days since listing (dividend-adjusted).
TestStatisticp-valueReading
ADF, log price0.210.973Unit root not rejected → prices are non-stationary
ADF, daily log returns-18.792.02e-30Stationary
Ljung-Box returns, lag 1017.620.0617No significant autocorrelation
Ljung-Box returns, lag 2029.090.0861
Ljung-Box squared returns, lag 10558.301.5e-113Volatility clustering
Engle ARCH-LM, 5 lags250.813.68e-52ARCH effects
Jarque-Bera normality5,500.730Non-normal (fat tails)

Reading the chart. The upper panel shows daily return autocorrelations inside the ±0.038 band at 16 of 20 lags, with the largest at 0.049 — no exploitable linear predictability, consistent with the Ljung-Box p = 0.06. The lower panel shows squared-return autocorrelation at 0.20 for lag 1, decaying slowly and remaining outside the band at 14 of 20 lags. The contrast is the standard signature of volatility clustering: the direction of the next move is unpredictable while its size is partly predictable, which supports sizing positions for tail risk rather than forecasting the price.

Calculated Log prices are non-stationary (ADF p = 0.97) while returns are stationary. Returns show no significant autocorrelation at ten lags (Ljung-Box p = 0.06), but squared returns are strongly autocorrelated and the ARCH-LM test confirms volatility clustering (p < 0.001). Excess kurtosis is 7.0; moves beyond three standard deviations happen on 1.8% of days, 6.8x what a normal distribution implies. Interpretation Past returns do not predict the direction of the next move, but they do predict its magnitude. That is why this report describes price action and sizes scenarios instead of forecasting the share price, and why position sizing should assume fat tails such as the −15% and +20% days in the event table.

Concentration of the outperformance in a five-month window is what the report means by a re-rating: the change is in the multiple applied to the same business, and it coincides with the Juniper close and the Q2 and Q3 FY26 results rather than being spread across the period.

The logarithmic scale means the vertical gap between HPE and Dell is a constant ratio, not a constant dollar amount, so Dell's lead is roughly a doubling relative to HPE over the window — the same ordering as the measured revenue elasticities (0.84 for Dell against 0.41 for HPE).

Reading the chart. Realised volatility is mean-reverting within a 25–45% band for most of the sample, punctuated by spikes: 126% in April 2020 and about 100% after the June 2026 move. It ends at 63%, roughly double the pre-2026 level. The clustering visible here is the same property the ARCH-LM test measures (p < 0.001), and it is the reason the report gives valuation ranges and scenario weights rather than a point target: with volatility at this level, a one-standard-deviation quarterly move is a large fraction of the gap between the price and the base-case value.

7 · News, filings, events & sentimentEarnings and guidance produce the largest price reactions; insiders sold into the re-rating

Material developments

  • Reported Q3 FY26 (2-Sep-2026): revenue $12.2bn (+34%), non-GAAP EPS $1.11, FCF $958m; FY26 and FY27 outlooks raised; dividend $0.1425 per quarter S063.
  • Reported Oracle collaboration: multi-year global deployment of HPE Juniper PTX/MX routing and QFX/EX switching with support and financing; HPE issued Oracle a warrant dated 2-Jul-2026 for up to 4,156,466 shares at $0.01, vesting in tranches on purchase milestones S001S151.
  • Reported Hyperscaler inference award: a $3.5bn traditional-server deal for the customer's internal inference use, signed after quarter-end S065.
  • Reported Portfolio: remaining H3C stake sold ($1.36bn, May-2026); Telco Solutions business sold (August 2026); court approved the DOJ settlement (August 2026) S066.
  • Reported Financing: $2.0bn senior notes (March 2026); term loan retired; $1.25bn notes to be repaid September 2026; S-8 for additional plan shares (June 2026).
  • Reported Governance: Elliott partner Chris Hsu joined the board (June 2026) under the July-2025 cooperation agreement S185.

Commercial agreements: what they could be worth

Estimate Oracle. The warrant is worth about $258m at $62.09. If it represents a 2–5% customer incentive — typical of equity-linked supply agreements, and our assumption, not a disclosure — it would correspond to roughly $5–13bn of cumulative purchases over several years, or $1–3bn a year against TTM Networking revenue of $11.0bn. Management places the "beginning" of the deal inside FY27 networking growth of 14–17%. Interpretation Margin should be at or above the segment average for routing, less the warrant cost, which we expect to be recognised against revenue as consideration payable to a customer (the accounting has not been confirmed in the reviewed filings). The uncertainty is high: tranche milestones and deployment timing are undisclosed.

Estimate $3.5bn inference deal. Equal to about 12% of TTM Cloud & AI revenue. At an assumed 6–10% operating margin for large server deals, it would add roughly $0.2–0.35bn of operating profit over its delivery period, mostly in FY27, with a temporary working-capital build.

Experiment 6 Earnings-day permutation test. Hypothesis. If earnings and guidance carry most of the news, HPE should move much more on earnings reaction days than on other days in the same period. Method. Mean absolute day-0 return on the 11 earnings reaction days against the other trading days since the first of them; p-value from 20,000 random draws of 11 non-earnings days (a permutation test), with a Mann-Whitney test as a check. The event table above is descriptive, not a formal event study. Data. Yahoo Finance adjusted prices, 1-Mar-2024 to 11-Sep-2026 (11 earnings days, 624 other days); reaction days from 8-K filing times.

Calculated Earnings days moved the stock 6.7% on average, 3.4 times the 2.0% of other days in the same period (permutation p < 0.001; Mann-Whitney p < 0.001). Interpretation Earnings and guidance dominate. The Juniper milestones produced smaller, mixed reactions (−8.0% excess on the leak, +14.5% on the DOJ settlement), and the September 2024 preferred offering cost the stock −6.5% relative in three days, consistent with its dilution.

Assumption Assumptions are tied to evidence: FY27 growth and margin to the raised framework (base) or its range edges; the bear's FY28 revenue decline mirrors the reversal of memory-driven ASP inflation that TrendForce expects to continue only "at a moderating pace" into 2027; the long-term margin range of 10.5–14.5% spans HPE's pre-Juniper mix-adjusted history to its FY27 guide; terminal growth brackets nominal GDP-like growth and stays below the 4.95% risk-free rate.

Reading the chart. In FY2027 the three scenarios differ by about $1.1bn of unlevered free cash flow ($4.1bn bear, $4.9bn base, $5.2bn bull). By FY2036 the spread is roughly $4.6bn ($4.1bn, $6.5bn, $8.7bn). The bear path is the only non-monotonic one: it falls to about $3.5bn by FY2029 as margin reverts to 10.5%, then grows with revenue. Because the paths separate gradually, scenario value is driven by the persistence of margin and growth rather than by the first forecast year, which is why the long-term margin assumption dominates the sensitivity analysis.

Reading the chart. Three drivers produce ranges of $12–14 per share: WACC ±1.0pp ($32.98–$46.66), revenue growth ±2pp p.a. ($32.84–$45.70) and long-term non-GAAP margin ±1.5pp ($32.72–$44.60). Two produce about $1: terminal growth ±0.5pp and net working capital ±3pp of the change in revenue. The asymmetry follows from the structure of the model: the discount rate and the margin apply to every forecast year and to the terminal value, whereas terminal growth is damped by the reinvestment needed to sustain it. No single adverse flex takes the value to the $62.09 price.

Calculated The largest valuation swings come from the discount rate ($33–$47 for ±1pp), annual growth ($33–$46 for ±2pp) and long-term margin ($33–$45 for ±1.5pp). Terminal growth and working-capital intensity matter far less. Interpretation Of these, long-term margin is the variable with the widest range of supportable values — which is why margin durability is the centre of the thesis.

11 · Investment synthesisA better HPE, priced as if the cycle were permanent

Business quality and moat. Interpretation HPE is a more attractive business than at any point since its separation: networking now produces 40% of segment profit, and trailing ROIC finally exceeds the cost of capital. The moat remains narrow and confined to networking and storage IP; servers, half the revenue, are a scale business in which HPE is losing share.

Growth and industry position. Reported Demand is real and visible — $7.6bn AI backlog, record orders, a raised FY27 framework — supported by an AI capex cycle running at more than half a trillion dollars a year. Interpretation HPE participates with a smaller share than Dell or Supermicro but with a broader enterprise and sovereign customer base, which is likely to prove more durable.

Financial health, cash and dilution. Calculated Leverage is back to 1.8x, TTM FCF is a record $4.5bn, and dilution from the preferred and warrants is under 10%. The weak spot is working capital: inventory has almost doubled and is financed by suppliers.

Management and capital allocation. Interpretation Execution in FY26 has been strong, and the Elliott-backed board has sharpened focus. But the long-run record — impairments and sub-WACC returns — argues for evidence before credit for the Juniper returns.

Stock behaviour and catalysts. Calculated The stock broke a decade-long range in April 2026 and is consolidating near all-time highs with volatility contracting. Near-term catalysts are the Networking Investor Day (30-Sep-2026), Q4 FY26 results and full FY27 guidance (early December 2026), and the preferred conversion (September 2027).

What the market appears to be pricing in

At $62.09: 13.5x FY27 EPS, a fully diluted market value $89.7bn equal to about 18x the ≥$5bn FY27 FCF framework, and in DCF terms either a 18% long-term operating margin, 11% annual growth for a decade, or a 7.0% discount rate. In short: that FY26–FY27 AI-cycle economics persist and that HPE deserves part of the AI-hardware peer multiple.

What the fundamental evidence suggests

Intrinsic value of $35–$43 per share in our base case (probability-weighted $38, bull $54), corroborated by the Damodaran model and HPE's own valuation history. Relative value is higher ($67–$106) only if today's sector multiples hold. The price therefore rests more on multiple persistence than on demonstrated cash flows.

What would change the conclusion

  • Upward: Cloud & AI margin holding ≥13% through a memory-price decline; Networking growing mid-teens organically at ≥25% margins with Oracle and Helios volumes; FY27 FCF well above $5bn with inventory normalising. Together these would lift the long-term margin toward 15% and our range toward $55–60.
  • Downward: non-GAAP gross margin back below 33%, sequential AI backlog decline, networking share loss in Dell'Oro data, or a sector de-rating as AI capex slows — each moves value toward the $22–35 bear-to-low-base range.

12 · Practitioner Q&AQuestions from the field, revised and answered

Questions raised while discussing this report. Each is restated in precise terminology, answered with the same evidence labels as the rest of the report, and tied back to what it means for HPE.

Q1 · Why would a data-centre SOP single out Juniper equipment?

As asked: “I was working as an IT engineer in the data center, in our SOP, when installing Juniper networking devices, we need to report to specific people in the company: does this imply that Juniper device have special properties, that other networking devices do not have?”

Revised question. In the data centre where I worked as an IT engineer, our standard operating procedure (SOP) required us to notify designated personnel whenever Juniper Networks equipment was installed. Does this imply that Juniper devices have technical, security or compliance characteristics that other network equipment lacks?

Terminology. “Report to specific people” becomes notify designated stakeholders, typically the change advisory board, the network security team or asset and licence management. “Networking devices” becomes network equipment: routers, switches, firewalls and wireless access points. “Special properties” becomes distinctive technical, security, licensing or regulatory characteristics. The SOP’s own rationale is not documented here, so the answer sets out the plausible reasons and how to confirm which one applies.

Short answer

Interpretation Not in the sense of unique hardware. Juniper routers, switches and firewalls run a proprietary operating system (Junos OS) and, in high-end routers, Juniper-designed silicon, but they do the same job as Cisco or Arista equipment and speak the same standard protocols. A vendor-specific notification step is better read as a signal of how the equipment is governed: its position in the network, the vendor’s security history, how it is licensed and managed, and — since 2-Jul-2025 — who owns the vendor. Each reason also applies to other vendors; the combination is what makes Juniper a sensible candidate for a named step.

Plausible reasons an SOP names Juniper, and whether each is specific to Juniper.
ReasonWhat applies to JuniperSpecific to Juniper?Evidence
Network role (blast radius)In data centres Juniper equipment typically serves as core and edge routers (MX, PTX), perimeter firewalls (SRX) and switching fabrics (QFX). A faulty change there can cut off many systems at once, so network and security owners want to know before a device goes live.No. Any core or perimeter device normally goes through change control.Interpretation
Security historyUnauthorised code inserted into ScreenOS, disclosed in 2015, created an administrative backdoor and allowed passive decryption of VPN traffic S215. A chain of unauthenticated J-Web vulnerabilities on EX switches and SRX firewalls was exploited in 2023 S217. The China-nexus espionage group UNC3886 installed custom backdoors on end-of-life MX routers; Mandiant disclosed this in March 2025 S216.Partly. Deliberate implants are unusual, but every large vendor has actively exploited vulnerabilities (Figure 31).Reported
Fast exposure checksWhen CISA adds a flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue, U.S. federal agencies get a remediation deadline. The deadline was three weeks for CVE-2025-21590 (added 13-Mar-2025, due 3-Apr-2025) and four days for the 2023 J-Web flaws S214, and many private operators follow the same catalogue. Meeting such deadlines requires a current list of every Juniper device with its software version and end-of-life status; notification at installation keeps that list current.No. The same logic applies to any vendor on a security watch list.Reported Interpretation
Integrity verificationMandiant advised upgrading to current Junos images and running the Juniper Malware Removal Tool (JMRT) quick scan and integrity check S216. A security team may want that procedure run at commissioning.The tool is Juniper-specific; verifying firmware integrity is general practice.Reported
Cloud management and data flowsSwitches, access points and SRX firewalls managed through Juniper Mist connect out to Mist cloud services on TCP 443 and TCP 2200, and SRX firewalls send logs on TCP 6514 S219. That needs firewall rules and often a review of what telemetry leaves the site.No. Cisco Meraki and HPE Aruba Central have similar requirements.Reported
Export classificationBefore Release 15.1, Junos packages came as “domestic” and “worldwide” editions that differed in the encryption allowed under U.S. export rules S218. The edition installed matters for sites outside the U.S. and Canada.No. Encryption export controls apply to all vendors’ software.Reported
Change of ownershipHPE completed the Juniper acquisition on 2-Jul-2025. The DOJ settlement required HPE to divest Instant On and auction a licence to Juniper’s Mist AI Ops source code S221. Support contracts, licence portals, approved-supplier records and account teams change as a result.Yes today, but temporary and administrative.Reported
Legal restrictionNot a reason. The U.S. Covered List and NDAA Section 889 restrictions name Huawei, ZTE, Hytera, Hikvision and Dahua S220. Juniper is a U.S. vendor and is not covered.—Reported

What the vulnerability data shows

Experiment 7 Exploited-vulnerability counts. Hypothesis. If the SOP singled out Juniper because its equipment is unusually exposed, Juniper should stand out in how often attackers exploit its flaws. Method. Count of entries in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue for 13 enterprise network and security vendors: in total, added since 2024, and flagged for known ransomware use. Counts are not normalised for installed base. Data. CISA KEV catalogue version 2026.09.11 (1,709 entries).

Reading the chart. The distribution is skewed: Cisco has 97 entries, 37% of the group total, followed by Ivanti (35) and Fortinet (30). Juniper has 8, ranking 8th of 13 vendors and below the group median of 12, with only 2 added since 2024 and none flagged for known ransomware use. Because the counts are not normalised for installed base, they cannot show that Juniper devices are safer per unit; they do show that Juniper is not an outlier in how often its flaws are exploited, which is the question the SOP raises.

Calculated Juniper has 8 of the catalogue’s 1,709 entries. That ranks 8th of the 13 enterprise network and security vendors compared, below the group median of 12 and far below Cisco (97), Ivanti (35) and Fortinet (30) S214. Only 2 Juniper entries were added since 2024, against 29 for Cisco and 19 for Fortinet. One of the two is the 2015 ScreenOS backdoor, added retroactively in October 2025. None of Juniper’s entries is flagged for known ransomware use; Fortinet has 14 and SonicWall 13.

Interpretation The counts are not normalised for installed base, and Cisco’s base is far larger, so they do not show Juniper devices to be safer per unit. They do show that Juniper is not an outlier in how often its flaws are exploited. What sets Juniper apart is the kind of incident. In 2015 unknown attackers modified the ScreenOS source code, and in 2025 a China-nexus espionage group planted backdoors on Junos routers. Incidents like these lead security teams to keep a named inventory and a named contact.

How to confirm the reason in your own organisation

  • Ask the SOP owner which control the step implements: change management (approval by the change advisory board), security (vulnerability or integrity baseline), asset and licence management (serial number and support entitlement) or procurement (supplier record).
  • Check whether other core or perimeter vendors have the same step. If only Juniper does, the likely origin is a past incident, an audit finding or a customer contract clause.
  • Check whether the named recipients changed after July 2025. An HPE support or account contact points to the ownership change.

Why it matters for HPE investors

  • Calculated The Juniper acquisition made networking 26% of HPE revenue and 40% of segment profit. Reported HPE’s FY2025 10-K warns that acquired companies may bring cybersecurity vulnerabilities, gaps or different security standards S029.
  • Interpretation The KEV record does not support a structural security discount on Juniper relative to Cisco, Fortinet or Palo Alto Networks. The risk is event-driven: a new implant-style compromise of Juniper routers would arrive while HPE is cross-selling Juniper into its server and Aruba accounts, and could slow orders from government and critical-infrastructure customers.
  • Interpretation The same history is also a refresh driver. The 2025 campaign targeted end-of-life routers, and Mandiant’s advice to plan end-of-life replacement points customers toward current MX and PTX routers and Mist-managed platforms, which is revenue for HPE Networking.
  • Interpretation Governance steps like this SOP add friction to deployments, but they also embed Juniper in customers’ operating processes and raise switching costs. That is consistent with the narrow networking moat described in Section 5. Mist AI Ops is the main differentiator, and the DOJ-mandated source-code licence makes it less exclusive S221.
  • Indicators to monitor: new Juniper or HPE entries in the KEV catalogue; out-of-cycle Juniper security advisories; networking order growth and segment margin; security and integration commentary at the Networking Investor Day on 30-Sep-2026.

Q2 · Landlords, neoclouds or server providers: what changes for the investor?

As asked: “the difference of investing in landlord (coreweave, keel infrastructure, digital reality) and investing in server providers (what are inside the data center)? What are properties / patterns of financial performance of these two types of business model (fixed cost, ratio of non-current asset on balance sheet, amortization for decreasing earnings, ...) (for landlord there is a large phase shift between cost and revenue recognition) (contracted based for land lord vs product based)? How do they likely be benefitted from AI boom (which one is more elastic)? Do you think it is a good idea to invest both or only one has Pareto frontier from financial perspective?” Follow-up: “make the comparison between three types of business model: landlord (digital reality, keel infrastructure), neocloud (iren, coreweave, nebius), and server providers (HPE, DELL).”

Revised question. How does investing in three layers of the AI data-centre supply chain differ: landlords that develop and lease powered data-centre space (Digital Realty, Keel Infrastructure), neoclouds that own GPU clusters and rent out computing capacity under multi-year contracts (IREN, CoreWeave, Nebius), and server providers that sell the equipment inside the building (HPE, Dell)? (1) How do their financial profiles differ in operating leverage, capital intensity (non-current assets as a share of total assets), depreciation, the lag between capital spending and revenue recognition, and contracted versus transactional revenue? (2) Which model's revenue, profit and share price are most sensitive to AI infrastructure spending? (3) Does combining the models improve the risk–return trade-off, or does one model dominate on the mean–variance efficient frontier?

Terminology. “Digital Reality” is Digital Realty. CoreWeave is not a landlord: it rents space and power from landlords, buys servers and sells compute, so the comparison has three tiers rather than two. “Amortization for decreasing earnings” is mainly depreciation of property and equipment (amortisation applies to intangibles and leasehold improvements), and the key judgement is the assets' useful life. The “phase shift between cost and revenue recognition” is the capex-to-revenue lag, or J-curve: construction cost is capitalised, depreciation starts only when an asset is placed in service, and rent is recognised over the lease. “Contracted vs product-based” is recurring contracted revenue (leases and take-or-pay capacity contracts, measured by remaining performance obligations or backlog) against point-in-time product revenue recognised on shipment. “More elastic” means a higher elasticity of revenue, profit or share price to AI capital spending. In portfolio terms the “Pareto frontier” is the mean–variance efficient frontier: portfolios for which no other portfolio offers a higher expected return for the same risk.

Short answer

Interpretation The three models are paid from the same AI capex dollar at different times and with different risks. Server providers book it as revenue almost at once, at single-digit operating margins, and need a new order for every future dollar. Landlords receive it as rent over many years, with heavy depreciation and debt but very stable revenue: Digital Realty's has not fallen year on year since 2018. Neoclouds sit between the two on timing but at the extreme on capital intensity, depreciation, leverage and share-price sensitivity. Revenue is most elastic at server providers; share prices are most elastic at neoclouds. On 17 months of common data, no single model is efficient on its own except at the highest-risk end. The least risky mix combined landlords with server providers; the best risk-adjusted mix combined server providers with neoclouds. Owning more than one model is justified, but which pair depends on the objective, and the return estimates behind it are fragile.

1 · Financial profile

Reading the chart. The three business models separate cleanly on every measure, which is the evidence that they are distinct models rather than variations of one. Neoclouds spend 2.7–8.2x revenue on capital expenditure while server providers spend at most 0.06x; depreciation plus interest consumes 67–74% of neocloud revenue against 3–10% for server providers; contracted backlog is 13.7–27.7x revenue for neoclouds and 0.3–0.9x for server providers. GAAP operating margin runs from −194% (Keel, pre-revenue development) to +14% (Digital Realty) and +6–9% for the server providers. The ordering of the bars is the same in the capex, depreciation and backlog panels, which is what a common underlying structure — capital committed ahead of revenue — looks like in the accounts.

Nebius: keyed from its 20-F and 6-K. IREN: contracted = RPO plus contracted lease value.

Calculated Capital intensity separates owners from sellers. Property, equipment and leased assets make up 62% of Digital Realty's balance sheet and 82% of CoreWeave's, against 9% at HPE and 6% at Dell S222 S223 S224 S225 S123 S124. Capex was 8.2x, 4.2x and 2.7x revenue at Nebius, IREN and CoreWeave, 0.5x at Digital Realty and 0.06x and 0.02x at HPE and Dell S238 S241. The broader non-current share discriminates less: HPE's is 59% because of goodwill and financing receivables, and IREN's and Keel's are low because they hold cash raised for construction.

Calculated Depreciation is where an owner's profit goes. Digital Realty earned an EBITDA margin of 44% but an operating margin of 14% after depreciation of 29% of revenue S245 S247. CoreWeave's EBITDA margin was 50%; depreciation (53% of revenue) and interest (21%) turned it into an operating margin of −3% and a net loss. At HPE and Dell depreciation is 8% and 2% of revenue and operating margins are thin but positive (6% and 9%), because most costs are components that rise and fall with sales. IREN's −148% and Keel's −194% also include bitcoin-mining impairments and accelerated depreciation S244 S248.

Calculated Contracts and cash point in opposite directions. Neoclouds hold contracted backlog of 13.7x (CoreWeave), 23.3x (IREN) and 27.7x (Nebius) their TTM revenue S236 S243 S242, but free cash flow of −435% to −127% of revenue while they build. Server providers hold less than a year of revenue in backlog (0.3x and 0.9x) and generate positive free cash flow (10% and 6%). Digital Realty sits between, with an estimated 5.3x its revenue under lease Estimate and free cash flow of −7% after development spending.

Calculated Stability follows the contracts. Over 32 quarters from 2018, Digital Realty's TTM revenue never fell year on year (weakest +1.4%). HPE's fell in 31% of quarters (worst −9.9%) and Dell's in 32% (worst −13.6%) S222 S123 S124.

Estimate Useful life is the neoclouds' biggest accounting judgement. Re-running CoreWeave's TTM depreciation on 5- or 4-year GPU lives instead of 6 would move its operating margin from −3% to −12% or −26%. Nebius, which lengthened server lives from four to five years in January 2026, would be at −64% on the old basis instead of −50% S235 S242. Straight-line proxy on the GPU share of depreciation; cash flow is unchanged, only the timing of expense moves.

2 · The phase shift

Reported In the filings, the lag shows up as leases signed but not yet paying (Digital Realty: $1.9bn of annual rent, nine months on average from signing to commencement S245), as assets not yet depreciated (construction in progress of $11.9bn at CoreWeave, $7.8bn of Nebius assets not yet in use, $65m at Keel) and as capitalised interest ($79m in CoreWeave's Q2) S236 S242 S248.

Experiment 8 Stylised 100 MW unit economics. Question. For the same 100 MW of AI capacity, who pays first and who books profit first? Method. A stylised quarterly cash-flow and GAAP operating-profit model for each business model, with parameters from company disclosures and one industry benchmark (table below). It illustrates timing and is not an estimate: it omits financing, taxes, re-leasing and residual values. Data. Digital Realty, CoreWeave, Nebius, IREN and Dell filings; JLL build-cost benchmark.

Reading the chart. The three models pay and earn at different times. The landlord's cumulative cash falls to −1.0x of capital during the 18-month build, then rises in a straight line at about 0.05x a year and only reaches breakeven near year 11.5, because rent is fixed at a 10% stabilised yield on cost. The neocloud falls to −1.0x when the GPUs are bought, recovers to positive by about year 3.2, and steps down again at the year-7 refresh when the next cluster is purchased. The server provider's line is the flat one, and the flatness is structural rather than a lack of sensitivity: the model contains a single shipment per six-year refresh cycle, so cash moves only twice — −1.0x when inventory is funded a quarter before shipment, then +0.18x when the customer pays a quarter after it — and there are no contracted flows in between. Its exposure therefore appears in the timing and size of the steps, not in the slope, and empirically in the 0.41 elasticity of revenue to hyperscaler capex. Over twelve years the server provider accumulates 0.35x of capital in operating profit against 3.2x for the neocloud, because it earns one margin per unit sold while the neocloud earns contracted revenue on the same hardware for five years.

Assumptions of the stylised 100 MW model (Assumption). It omits financing, taxes, re-leasing and residual values: its purpose is the timing, not the returns.
ModelParameters
LandlordFacility cost $17.5m per MW (AI-optimised builds $15–20m+ S251); 18-month build; 10% stabilised yield on cost (Digital Realty guidance S245); 25-year straight-line depreciation
NeocloudRevenue $22.5m per MW per year (Nebius $20–25m S240); 59% EBITDA margin (CoreWeave adjusted, Q2 2026 S237); GPU capex of $26.5m per MW, set so EBITDA repays it in two years (IREN's “~2-year payback” S244); 5-year contract and 6-year depreciation S235, then 40% of the price until the refresh
Server providerSells those GPU systems at a 15% operating margin (Dell ISG, Q2 FY27 S250); inventory bought a quarter before shipment, cash collected a quarter after

Calculated The model reproduces the phase shift. The landlord books operating profit from the quarter the building goes live, but cash does not repay the building for about 11.5 years: after 12 years cumulative operating profit is 0.63x the capital but cumulative cash only 0.05x. The neocloud reaches cash payback in about 3.2 years if its GPUs stay contracted, and ends at 3.0x; a four-year depreciation life lowers its reported cumulative profit only from 3.2x to 3.0x, mostly by moving profit between years. The server provider gets its cash back within two quarters of shipment but earns only 0.18x per deployment, and needs the next refresh order to earn again.

Calculated Interpretation In Digital Realty's own history the lag is not visible at annual-growth frequency. Growth in TTM development capex and in TTM revenue is most correlated in the same quarter (0.67) and most negatively correlated 6 quarters apart (−0.51) S222, because acquisitions and joint-venture contributions add both at once. The contractual lag lives in the backlog rather than in reported growth.

3 · Which model benefits more from the AI boom?

Experiment 9 Elasticity of revenue and share price to AI demand. Hypothesis. Revenue recognised at shipment should respond most to hyperscaler capex, while share prices should respond most where operating and financial leverage are highest. Method. (1) Revenue elasticity: quarterly OLS of each company's year-over-year log revenue growth on hyperscaler capex growth, lags 0–4, Newey-West errors and t-distribution p-values; the elasticity is the sum of the lags (joint t-test), and a regression of Dell's minus HPE's growth tests whether the two differ. (2) Share-price sensitivity: daily returns on four factors — the S&P 500, an AI factor (NVIDIA's return not explained by the S&P 500), bitcoin and the 10-year yield — with Newey-West errors. Data. SEC XBRL, 2018Q2–2026Q2 (33 quarters) for Digital Realty, HPE and Dell; Yahoo Finance and FRED daily data, 31-Mar-2025 to 11-Sep-2026.

Reading the chart. The AI-factor panel separates the groups: CoreWeave 0.85 and Nebius 0.81 with intervals well clear of zero, IREN 0.40 (p = 0.02), against HPE 0.02 and Dell 0.18 whose intervals span zero. The market-beta panel shows the opposite ordering of precision — every estimate is significant, with neoclouds and Keel at 2.5–2.9 and server providers at 1.7–2.0. Bitcoin betas are indistinguishable from zero for all seven names, including the former miners. Only Digital Realty has a significant rate sensitivity, −0.6% per +10bp, consistent with a long-duration lease book. Interval width, not bar length, is what distinguishes a measured exposure from an unmeasured one here.

Revenue elasticity: quarterly year-over-year log revenue growth on the capex growth of Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle, lags 0–4, 2018Q2–2026Q2 (n = 33), Newey-West errors, t-distribution p-values. Share-price betas: daily returns 2025-03-31 to 2026-09-11, Newey-West errors; AI factor = NVIDIA return not explained by the S&P 500; bold = significant at 5%. Calculated.

Calculated Revenue responds fastest at server providers. A 10-point rise in hyperscaler capex growth has gone with 8.4 points of revenue growth at Dell and 4.1 at HPE over five quarters, mostly in the same quarter. The gap between them is significant (0.43, p = 0.004), and controlling for Juniper cuts HPE's to 0.09 (p = 0.45). Digital Realty shows no significant link (0.06, p = 0.56) S169 S170 S171 S172 S173 S222 S123 S124. The neoclouds are too new for a regression, but their revenue grew 115% (CoreWeave, TTM), 41% (IREN, TTM, still mostly bitcoin mining) and 529% (Nebius, first half), against 81% growth in hyperscaler capex S225 S224 S241.

Calculated Share prices tell a different story. Net of the market, CoreWeave and Nebius moved 0.85% and 0.81% for each 1% of NVIDIA's AI-specific return and IREN 0.40%, against 0.18% for Dell, 0.02% for HPE and 0.03% for Digital Realty, none of them significantly different from zero. Neoclouds and Keel also carry market betas of 2.5–2.9, against 1.7–2.0 for the server providers and 0.7 for Digital Realty. Digital Realty is the only name with a significant rate sensitivity (−0.6% per +10bp) S228 S229 S230 S231 S232 S129 S132 S233 S130 S234 S166.

Interpretation Both answers are right, for different questions. Server providers have the most elastic revenue because they recognise it at shipment. Neoclouds have the most elastic equity because operating and financial leverage turn small changes in expected AI demand into large changes in what is left after debt. Landlords are the least elastic on both measures, and their AI gain shows up first in bookings, backlog and renewal rents (Digital Realty reported cash rent increases of 25.4% on renewals in Q2 2026 S245) and in the value of powered land (Keel's 2.2 GW pipeline S249). Keel's high market beta still reflects its bitcoin-mining past.

4 · One model or several?

Experiment 10 Portfolio construction. Hypothesis. If the three business models carry different risks, a mix should beat owning any one of them on risk, return or both. Method. Equal-weighted daily baskets per model; long-only minimum-variance and maximum-Sharpe weights and the efficient frontier; the two-asset threshold below to see when one model makes another redundant; weights re-estimated on 2,000 stationary block-bootstrap resamples (20-day blocks) to see how stable they are. Data. Yahoo Finance daily returns, 31-Mar-2025 to 11-Sep-2026, with two robustness windows; 3-month bill rate from FRED.

Reading the chart. In the left panel the efficient frontier runs from 48.5% volatility and 113% return to 91% and 174%. The landlord basket (60% volatility, 91% return) and the server basket (56%, 131%) lie below the frontier, so a combination of them dominates either alone; the neocloud basket lies on the frontier but only at its riskiest end. The minimum-variance point sits at 48.5% volatility, lower than any individual basket, which is the diversification result. The right panel shows how stable those weights are: server-provider weights centre near 56% with a wide distribution, landlord weights near 44%, and neocloud weights are below 1% in 97% of the 2,000 resamples. The weights come from seventeen months of an AI upcycle, so the covariance ordering is more reliable than the mean returns behind the maximum-Sharpe point.

Baskets are equal-weighted and rebalanced daily; weights are long-only; risk-free rate = average 3-month bill yield. Main: 31-Mar-2025 to 11-Sep-2026. Digital Realty only: same window with Digital Realty as the landlord basket. Longer window: from 22-Oct-2024 (CoreWeave joins at its IPO). Calculated.

When does one model make another redundant? For two assets with volatilities σlow ≤ σhigh and correlation ρ, the minimum-variance weight in the lower-volatility asset is w* = (σhigh² − ρσlowσhigh) / (σlow² + σhigh² − 2ρσlowσhigh). Adding the riskier asset lowers risk only if ρ < σlow/σhigh; otherwise the least risky portfolio holds the safer asset alone.

Calculated Landlords and neoclouds sit at or beyond this threshold: ρ = 0.66 against a volatility ratio of 0.66 in the main window (so the neocloud weight is only 0.1%), 0.69 against 0.62 from October 2024, and 0.37 against 0.28 with Digital Realty alone. Server providers pass against both (ρ = 0.39 against 0.94; 0.40 against 0.62). The long-only minimum-variance portfolio therefore holds landlords (45%) and server providers (55%) and no neoclouds. In 2,000 bootstrap resamples, neoclouds received no minimum-variance weight in 97% of draws, while landlords and server providers always received some S130 S167.

Calculated The maximum-Sharpe portfolio, which also uses average returns, holds server providers (72%) and neoclouds (28%) and no landlords. That result is fragile: landlords received zero weight in 51% of resamples, neoclouds in 18% and server providers in 2%; all three models appeared together in 38%. With Digital Realty as the only landlord, the least risky mix is 93% Digital Realty and 7% server providers, and the maximum-Sharpe mix is unchanged.

Interpretation Answer. On this evidence the individual baskets are Pareto-inefficient. The server-provider and landlord baskets both sit below the frontier, so a mix delivers more return for their risk; only the neocloud basket touches the frontier, at its riskiest end (91% volatility, −49% drawdown). Owning more than one model beats owning one. The right pair depends on the objective: landlords with server providers to reduce risk, server providers with neoclouds to chase AI upside. Server providers appear in almost every efficient mix. The averages behind the maximum-Sharpe result come from an AI boom (annualised basket returns of 91% to 174%) and will not repeat; the covariance-based result is the more reliable of the two.

How each model fares in four AI-cycle scenarios (Interpretation, informed by the regressions above).
ScenarioLandlordsNeocloudsServer providers
AI capex keeps risingGradual gain: pre-leasing and higher renewal rents; revenue follows a year or more laterLargest gain: contracts fill fixed-cost capacity, and leverage amplifies the equityImmediate gain: shipments and backlog convert within quarters, at thin margins
Capex digestion (growth pauses)Least affected: rent is contracted; new developments slowHurt: fewer new contracts and costlier funding; existing backlog cushions revenueHurt most in revenue: orders fall first (HPE's and Dell's TTM revenue fell in 31% and 32% of quarters since 2018)
Oversupply or credit stressHurt at renewal and on unleased sites such as Keel's pipelineHurt most: GPUs lose value before debt is repaid; concentrated customersHurt through customer credit, receivables and inventory
Rates riseHurt most in valuation (Digital Realty −0.6% per +10bp)Refinancing costs rise; long contracts are worth lessLeast affected: no significant rate sensitivity

Interpretation The scenarios point the same way as the covariance data: each model is hurt most by a different shock (server providers by digestion, landlords by rates, neoclouds by credit stress), which is the case for owning more than one.

Why it matters for HPE investors

  • Calculated HPE's revenue elasticity to hyperscaler capex (0.41) is about half Dell's (0.84), a statistically significant gap (p = 0.004); its AI beta is 0.02 against Dell's 0.18, though neither is significantly different from zero. HPE gives less concentrated exposure to the server segment, with a larger networking and GreenLake mix.
  • Interpretation Neoclouds' negative free cash flow (−435% to −127% of revenue) is funded by debt, prepayments and vendor credit, so server providers that finance customers take on part of that risk. HPE Financial Services runs a $13.2bn portfolio at 7x leverage S029; its exposure to AI-cloud customers is worth watching.
  • Interpretation GreenLake and financing give HPE a small landlord-like, contracted revenue stream (ARR target of about $3.5bn S074 S066) inside a product business, which helps explain why its revenue has been less cyclical than Dell's.
  • Indicators to monitor: hyperscaler capex growth; neocloud prepayments and funding spreads; landlord backlog and renewal rents; changes to GPU useful-life policies.

Limitations

  • Short or transitional histories: CoreWeave has 17 months of prices and Nebius 23; IREN and Keel were bitcoin miners for most of their listed life, and their margins include mining impairments.
  • Two or three names per model: Keel accounts for most of the landlord basket's variance (Digital Realty alone had 26% volatility against 60% for the basket).
  • Nebius figures are keyed from its 20-F and 6-K; Digital Realty's contracted backlog is an estimate; HPE's TTM interest expense uses its last reported annual figure.
  • The stylised model ignores financing, taxes, re-leasing risk and residual values, and assumes the neocloud's GPUs stay contracted.
  • The frontier uses past returns from an AI boom: it shows what diversification did, not what it will do.

Limitations

  • Gartner, IDC and Dell'Oro full reports are paywalled; figures come from public releases or press coverage, noted where the release itself was not retrievable.
  • Consensus estimates and 13F compilations are from Yahoo Finance (secondary); social-media sentiment could not be collected.
  • Segment history on the FY26 structure covers only Q1 FY25–Q3 FY26; Q2 FY25 is derived from nine-month totals.
  • Juniper's contribution cannot be isolated precisely after integration; organic comparisons use company-normalised figures.
  • Debt benefiting Financial Services (~$11.5bn) is an analyst estimate from the disclosed 7.0x FS debt-to-equity ratio.
